AL: Riparian state: the owner of the land may make reasonable use of water that rises on it, shared with neighbors downstream. Ordinary household and farm use needs no permit.
AR: Riparian state: the owner of the land may make reasonable use of water that rises on it, shared with neighbors downstream. Ordinary household and farm use needs no permit. Diversions from streams must be registered each year with the state's Natural Resources Division.
AZ: Prior appropriation: spring water belongs to whoever holds a recorded water right, and that right can be owned separately from the land. A springhead without a right attached may come with little more than household use, so check the state's water-rights records for the spring before buying.
CA: California recognizes both riparian and appropriative rights, and springs that feed a stream can be subject to others' rights downstream. The State Water Board keeps the records.
CO: Prior appropriation: spring water belongs to whoever holds a recorded water right, and that right can be owned separately from the land. A springhead without a right attached may come with little more than household use, so check the state's water-rights records for the spring before buying.
FL: Water belongs to the state. Household use is exempt, but pumping more, including bottling, needs a consumptive-use permit from the regional water management district, and owning the spring doesn't guarantee one. Florida also sets minimum flows for major springs.
